blocks.text: Around 1300, in north-western Anatolia, a Turkish bey called Osman led one of the small principalities, *beylikler*, that had formed as the power of the Seljuks of Anatolia faded. The dynasty took its name from him: *Osmanlı* in Turkish, **Ottoman** in English, from Uthman, the Arabic form of his name. It would rule for more than six centuries.

Osman's son Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it his capital. In the following decades the Ottomans crossed into the Balkans, and from the 1360s Edirne served as their capital. In 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, and made it his own; the city's story is told in [a later interlude](b1-u08-culture).

Under Süleyman I (1520–1566), called *Kanuni*, the Lawgiver, in Turkish and **the Magnificent** in Europe, the empire was one of the great powers of the world. It ruled the Balkans and Anatolia, much of the Arab Middle East and North Africa, and its armies besieged Vienna in 1529, without taking it. It was a state of many peoples and faiths: Turks, Greeks, Armenians, Arabs, Kurds, Jews, Slavs and many others lived under the sultan.

A second siege of Vienna failed in 1683, and in the treaties that followed the empire began to lose land in Europe. Historians long called the next centuries a decline; many now describe a state that kept adapting, reorganizing its army, its laws and its finances. The reforms of the *Tanzimat*, from 1839, and the first constitution, in 1876, belong to this story, as does the Young Turk revolution of 1908, which restored the constitution.

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, national movements and wars cost the empire most of its Balkan lands. In 1914 it entered the First World War on the side of Germany. During the war, in 1915 and 1916, the Ottoman government deported the Armenians of Anatolia, and hundreds of thousands of them died. Most historians and many states call these events a genocide; the Turkish state rejects that term.

Defeated, the empire signed the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918, and Allied troops occupied Istanbul. A national movement led from Ankara by Mustafa Kemal won the War of Independence ([unit 1](a2-u01-culture)). On 1 November 1922 the Grand National Assembly in Ankara abolished the sultanate, and the last sultan, Mehmed VI, left Istanbul on 17 November. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, and the caliphate was abolished in March 1924.

The Ottoman centuries left their mark on the whole region, from Bosnia to Iraq: mosques, bridges and bazaars, much of the cooking, music and vocabulary, and a written language, Ottoman Turkish, in Arabic script, which the [1928 reform](a1-u01-culture) replaced.
Here is the empire on one page, in the Turkish of this unit:

blocks.tr: Osman Bey 1300'e doğru küçük bir beyliğin başındaydı. Oğlu Orhan Bey Bursa'yı alıp başkent yaptı. 1453'te Fatih Sultan Mehmet İstanbul'u aldı, ondan sonra İstanbul başkent oldu. Kanuni Sultan Süleyman padişahken imparatorluk çok büyüktü. Sonra imparatorluk yavaş yavaş küçüldü. En sonunda, 1922'de saltanat bitti.
blocks.en: Around 1300, Osman Bey was at the head of a small principality. His son Orhan Bey took Bursa and made it his capital. In 1453 Mehmed the Conqueror took Istanbul; after that, Istanbul became the capital. When Süleyman the Lawgiver was sultan, the empire was very large. Then the empire slowly grew smaller. In the end, in 1922, the sultanate came to an end.

vocab.en: principality, small state ruled by a bey
sultanate, the rule of a sultan
to be at the head of, to lead

questions.q: Which city did Orhan make his capital in 1326?
questions.explain: Bursa, then Edirne from the 1360s, then Istanbul from 1453.

questions.q: In the Turkish text, what does *Kanuni Sultan Süleyman padişahken* mean?
options: when Süleyman the Lawgiver was sultan
after Süleyman the Lawgiver became sultan
because Süleyman the Lawgiver was sultan
questions.explain: *padişah* + *-ken*: **while (he was) sultan**. The past comes from the main verb, *büyüktü*.

questions.q: When did the Grand National Assembly abolish the sultanate?
questions.explain: The sultanate ended on 1 November 1922; the Republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923.

sources.title: Ottoman Empire
sources.note: Dynasty founded by the bey Osman, about 1300 to 1922; peak of power 1481–1566; greatest extent around 1683–1699; Tanzimat 1839–1876; constitution of 1876; Young Turk revolution of 1908; disintegration after the First World War

sources.title: Ottoman Empire
sources.note: Osman I's principality in north-western Anatolia, about 1299; Orhan takes Bursa in 1326 and makes it the capital; Edirne the capital from the 1360s to 1453; 29 May 1453; Suleiman I 1520–1566 and the siege of Vienna in 1529; 1683; Tanzimat; 1876; 1908; entry into the war in 1914; Armistice of Mudros, 30 October 1918, and the occupation of Istanbul

sources.title: History of the Ottoman Empire
sources.note: The decline thesis and the later view of the 17th century as a period of adaptation rather than stagnation

sources.title: Abolition of the Ottoman sultanate
sources.note: Sultanate abolished by the Grand National Assembly on 1 November 1922; Mehmed VI left on 17 November 1922; Treaty of Lausanne 24 July 1923; caliphate abolished in March 1924

sources.title: Armenian Genocide
sources.note: A campaign of deportation and mass killing of the Armenian subjects of the Ottoman Empire by the Young Turk government during the First World War; the Turkish government rejects the term genocide

sources.title: Armenian genocide
sources.note: Deportations of 1915 and 1916; estimates of 600,000 to 1.5 million deaths; academic consensus and recognition by many states; the Turkish government's position
